section_summary: This section begins with the continuation of a State Department pamphlet explaining United States controls on arms, tin-plate scrap, and helium exports, including special restrictions relating to China, Cuba, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Spain. The remaining records document public, congressional, corporate, and advocacy-group pressure to halt exports useful to Japan’s war effort, together with State Department explanations of the limits of the Neutrality Act. They also include legal arguments for sanctions under tariff and treaty law and a statistical bulletin comparing 1937 and 1938 exports of strategic materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: International Traffic in Arms pamphlet, continued: special export provisions
subfiles.about: Continuation of a regulatory pamphlet explaining special United States export controls on arms, tin-plate scrap, and helium.
subfiles.summary: The pamphlet explains the requirement for importing-government approval of arms shipments to China, Cuba, Honduras, and Nicaragua and reproduces the statutory embargo applicable to Spain. It prints Franklin D. Roosevelt's May 1, 1937 proclamation enumerating controlled arms, aircraft, chemical agents, and explosives. Later sections reproduce the licensing rules and application forms governing exports of tin-plate scrap and helium gas.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to F. Thompson concerning exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Explains why the executive branch cannot prohibit exports of copper, brass, and machinery to Japan under existing law.
subfiles.summary: The draft directs Thompson to Department of Commerce trade statistics. It states that existing statutes permit restrictions only on articles formally enumerated as arms, ammunition, and implements of war, while assuring him that public views on foreign policy receive consideration.

subfiles.title: File copy of Sumner Welles's reply to F. Thompson
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: File copy of the State Department's explanation of its lack of authority to stop most strategic-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles explains that trade data can be obtained from the Department of Commerce and that neither the President nor the Secretary of State can bar ordinary commodities such as copper, brass, and machinery. He encloses a pamphlet containing the May 1, 1937 proclamation defining arms, ammunition, and implements of war.

subfiles.title: Mrs. McBride's message and enclosed clipping on aid to China
subfiles.about: A brief inquiry or protest concerning continuing American sales to Japan, accompanied by a clipping on Western aid to China.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. McBride's January 1939 message and clipping: Western aid strengthens Chinese morale, Japan bought most US scrap iron in November, and Chiang warned China might rely only on the Soviet Union.

subfiles.title: Reply to Mrs. McBride regarding exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the Neutrality Act's application to a possible formal finding of war between China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost tells Mrs. McBride a war proclamation would bar arms to both China and Japan; gives license values; the President used discretion by issuing none; non-munitions commodities are outside the act.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Aluminum Corporation cooperation with aircraft-export policy
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Records the Aluminum Corporation of America's decision to stop selling products that might be used in Japanese aircraft.
subfiles.summary: Aluminum Corporation officials describe sales through Japanese houses; since some products could be aircraft material, it decided to reject sales whenever aircraft use was possible; Yost expressed appreciation.

subfiles.title: Follow-up memorandum on rejected Japanese aluminum orders
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Reports documentary evidence that the Aluminum Corporation was rejecting Japanese orders for possible aircraft materials.
subfiles.summary: Simmons and Romney show telegrams proving substantial orders suited to aircraft were refused, while orders for unrelated products continued.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Colorado House Memorial No. 1
subfiles.from: Marvin H. McIntyre, Secretary to the President
subfiles.about: Refers the Colorado legislature's memorial on sales of war materials to Japan to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: White House forwards Colorado House Memorial No. 1 and correspondence to State.

subfiles.title: William C. Blair transmittal of Colorado House Memorial No. 1
subfiles.from: William C. Blair, Chief Clerk, Colorado House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Transmits an engrossed memorial asking the federal government to stop sales of munitions and war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Blair sends the President Colorado House Memorial No. 1 on munitions and war material sales to Japan.

subfiles.title: Colorado House Memorial No. 1
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: Calls for immediate action terminating American sales of munitions and war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Colorado House Memorial No. 1 argues denying Japan munitions would advance peace and impede the China war, asking Colorado's congressional delegation to support measures.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of Colorado House Memorial No. 1
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Colorado memorial and encloses a departmental statement on arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Moore thanks Blair for the memorial, promising careful consideration, with four copies of the Department's statement on exports to Japan and China.

subfiles.title: Senator McNary's inquiry concerning Joe E. Dunne's letter
subfiles.from: Charles L. McNary, United States Senator
subfiles.about: Requests information needed to answer Joe E. Dunne's question about sponge-iron exports under the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Senator McNary forwards Joe Dunne's letter, asking State for information and the enclosure's return.

subfiles.title: Joe E. Dunne inquiry about sponge-iron exports
subfiles.about: Asks whether a Japanese declaration of war against China would stop sponge-iron shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dunne asks whether sponge iron would become contraband or be barred under the Neutrality Act if Japan declared war on China; a substantial contract is at stake.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply on the status of sponge iron
subfiles.about: Explains how the Neutrality Act would affect sponge-iron exports following a formal finding of war between China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull says a Section 1 proclamation would bar arms exports to both belligerents but could not classify sponge iron as arms; further restrictions need a Section 2 finding.

subfiles.title: Harry B. Price letter transmitting a program memorandum
subfiles.from: Harry B. Price, American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: Transmits a memorandum proposing intensified activity to stop American economic aid to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Price thanks Hornbeck for a meeting and asks him to review a program memorandum, reporting growing support for ending economic aid to Japan.

subfiles.title: Some Practical Questions Pertaining to the Activities of the American Committee
subfiles.to: Members and cooperating organizations of the American Committee
subfiles.about: Considers the objectives and lobbying methods of a campaign to stop war supplies and credits to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Price weighs a broader program (tariff discrimination, gold policy, aid to China, British consultation) against focusing on halting war supplies; recommends building public and congressional sentiment first.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck reply concerning Price's program memorandum
subfiles.about: Acknowledges and comments favorably on Price's memorandum about the American Committee's activities.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Price for the memorandum, studied with interest, and offers to discuss it on Price's next visit.

subfiles.title: Price letter transmitting committee material and Quincy Wright's opinion
subfiles.about: Arranges a Washington meeting and confidentially transmits committee material and a legal opinion on restricting Japanese imports.
subfiles.summary: Price will visit Washington and encloses committee material and Quincy Wright's opinion on using tariff and customs law against Japanese imports.

subfiles.title: Quincy Wright opinion on tariff retaliation and sanctions against Japan
subfiles.to: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: Analyzes whether the President could legally restrict Japanese imports or impose an export embargo as a reprisal for treaty violations.
subfiles.summary: Wright concludes municipal law permits excluding Japanese goods under tariff provisions, though ordinary use may conflict with the 1911 treaty; Japan's treaty violations justify suspending treaty privileges by analogy to League sanctions on Italy.

subfiles.title: Extracts from Section 338 and Title 19, Section 181
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: Reproduces statutory provisions authorizing exclusion of imports from countries that discriminate against American commerce.
subfiles.summary: Extracts of Section 338 on foreign discrimination and Title 19, Section 181, letting the President exclude products from a discriminating state.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment of Price's January 20 enclosures
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Price's letter and thanks him for the enclosed information.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck acknowledges Price's January 20 letter and enclosure.

subfiles.title: Price letter transmitting Fred H. Lysons's treaty argument
subfiles.about: Transmits a Seattle lawyer's argument that withholding war supplies from Japan would fulfill United States obligations under the Nine-Power Treaty.
subfiles.summary: Price sends Hornbeck Fred Lysons's letter to Roger Greene, which may broaden the legal basis for stopping aid that enables Japan's treaty violations.

subfiles.title: Fred H. Lysons letter advocating executive action under the Nine-Power Treaty
subfiles.about: Argues that the President can and should stop war-material shipments to Japan as a direct fulfillment of the Nine-Power Treaty.
subfiles.summary: Lysons argues treaties are self-executing law and that knowingly allowing war-material shipments makes the US complicit in violating China's sovereignty, urging executive action and noting benefits of a reconstructed China.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment of the Lysons letter
subfiles.about: Acknowledges and comments on the copy of Fred H. Lysons's letter.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck acknowledges Price's February 3 letter enclosing Lysons's January 24 communication to Greene, read with interest.

subfiles.title: Sale of War Materials by the United States to Japan, January–November 1938
subfiles.about: Compares American exports to Japan of commodities considered essential for war during the first eleven months of 1938 and 1937.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin tabulates quantities, values, and percentage changes for hides, petroleum, iron and steel, nonferrous metals, machinery, vehicles, aircraft, arms, and ammunition. It reports major increases in such categories as crude petroleum, copper, lead, metal-working machinery, and aircraft and parts, while iron and steel semimanufactures declined. The figures were compiled from Department of Commerce foreign-trade statistics and assign a 1938 grand total of approximately $142 million to the listed commodities.
